_honestyNote:
WHAT THIS FILM IS ALLOWED TO CLAIM, AND WHY IT IS SHAPED LIKE THIS.

This repo cannot photograph a real scan. Two independent facts make that true, and both were checked against source rather than assumed:

  1. THE CAMERA FEED IS A CARTOON. Every `?mock=xr8` shot runs
     public/test-fixtures/xr8-mock.js, whose `drawScene` paints the 'room' with
     Canvas-2D fillRect/ellipse calls — a cyan TV, an orange sofa, a walnut
     table, a lollipop plant, on a two-stop wall gradient. It is a fixture for a
     colour-blob detector, not a photograph. It cannot be cropped out either:
     the HUD occupies about 0.23 of the plate width, which needs roughly a 4x
     push, and video-kit's MAX_SCALE is 2.4 (camera.mjs:64). At the tightest
     framing 16:9 permits, the top of the sofa and the TV are still in shot.
  2. THERE IS NO REAL CAPTURED GEOMETRY IN THE REPO TO SUBSTITUTE.
     worlds/default.json is an orphaned manifest: every glbUrl it lists under
     /scans/ is gone from the checkout (verified — 0 of its referenced GLBs
     resolve). It also carries a real street address and GPS fix in its
     geoPose blocks, so it should not be revived for filming as-is.

Capturing a real phone scan and committing it is the option that would fix this
properly. It is not available to this pipeline: there is no device, video-kit
captures product screens through Playwright only, and the house rule for these
films is that no footage may be shot that the pipeline cannot shoot. Faking one
was never on the table.

So the film re-frames and says less, which is the remaining honest pair:

  RE-FRAME. The claims that need real data — objects named, objects placed,
  one world, a map you own — are now made ONLY over the World Editor. That is
  the one surface where the product is doing real work on real data: three GLBs
  uploaded through the real /upload-scan path, put through the real optimize
  jobs, rendered as a real point cloud (69,046 points), carrying 15 real
  detections with real confidences and real metric dimensions. The rooms are
  generated fixtures rather than someone's house — that is a limit worth
  knowing — but the geometry, the pipeline and the readout are the product.

  SAY LESS. Four of the five scanner-over-cartoon shots are cut from this film
  outright: `detections-panel`, `objects-manifest`, `review-export-panel` and
  the single-shot uses of the live HUD. The previous cut carried the caption
  'Every object named, placed and yours.' over a frame whose objects were
  fillRect calls; that claim now lands on `one-world`, where fifteen genuinely
  detected objects are on screen.

  The ONE surviving mock frame is the `the-meter` scene, and it is deliberately
  a `split`: the same scripted session at tick 90 and at tick 700, side by side.
  Two identical rooms in two browser frames read as a controlled comparison
  rather than as somebody's living room, the subject becomes the coverage meter
  (which is a real product behaviour, computed from the real point count), and
  the caption says on the frame that the session is scripted. That is the only
  place in the film where the mock appears, and it is labelled where it appears.

The detector is also a mock: INFERENCE_MODE=mock is a colour-blob CV matcher
(inference.ts `_inferMock`), not the VLM the product ships. No scene in this cut
claims a vision model, names one, or shows its output — the confidences on
screen belong to the World Editor's stored detections.

scenes.title: How wide is that alcove?
scenes.caption: Four years here, and the answer is still: go and measure it.
scenes.narration: How wide is that alcove? You have lived here four years, and the honest answer is that you would have to go and measure it.
scenes._editNote: The pain, told concretely rather than as a category, and set as a spec sheet of unknowns — which is the beat: the room is the one thing in the house with no numbers attached to it. Typographic rather than a screen because the subject is an ABSENCE, and there is no product surface that shows the absence of data; inventing one would be the dishonesty this rewrite exists to remove. The three chips are also what keeps the card moving — see the note on `pain-not-a-file`.

scenes.title: Your house is not a file.
scenes.caption: Everything that happened in it is.
scenes.narration: Your photos are files. Your messages are files. The place all of it happened in is the one thing you have never captured.
scenes._editNote:
Chips carry no invented counts — "files" and "nothing", not a fabricated number of photos. The film may not put a statistic on screen that it did not measure.

These three cards were itemless in the first cut of this rewrite and it cost the film the frozen-picture gate: 11% landscape / 14% portrait against an 8% bar. `feature` renders `title` once and then holds, and both the paced reveal and the drift target the chips row (`.<id>-chips`) — with no chips there is literally nothing in motion. Every itemised feature in the fleet measures 0-3%. Do not strip the items back out.

scenes.title: Most people quit right about here.
scenes.caption: The usual price of a room you can measure.
scenes.narration: The tools that fix this want a lidar rig, a subscription, and a copy of your floor plan on somebody else's server. Most people quit right about here.

scenes.title: Companion Scan
scenes.caption: Walk the room. Keep the map.
scenes.narration: There is a shorter way, and it needs the phone already in your pocket.

scenes.caption: Two ways in. Both end in a map.
scenes.narration: Walk a room with the camera, or hand it a walkthrough video you already have.

shots.alt: Start screen offering two equal paths: scan a room, or upload a video
shots._focusNote:
The beat is the PAIR of cards, not the app's own title — we have just come off the title card, so re-reading the wordmark is dead weight.

A FOCUS RECTANGLE IS NOT THE WINDOW YOU GET, and every landscape y in this file is set from `ci-video focus-preview`'s reported window rather than from the rectangle. Measured: the delivered window lands 0.029 of the plate BELOW the authored y at scale 2.398. The browser frame is not centred on the canvas centre — the stage reserves the caption band, so frameCentre.y is 479.5 against a canvas centre of 540 — and the screenshot sits below the chrome inside the frame. Author a y from a rectangle alone and the crop arrives a couple of dozen plate pixels lower than the one you looked at.

Landscape: the two cards occupy x 0.381-0.619, y 0.518-0.735 — 0.24 wide, far under the 0.538 floor, so no rectangle frames them tighter and the floor square is authored directly (scale 2.398, honoured exactly, nothing clamped). y 0.376 delivers a window top of 0.405, which is chosen and not rounded: the descender of 'Companion' ends at 0.404 and the cap of 'Scan' starts at 0.407, so the crop lands in the gap BETWEEN the two wordmark lines. Verified on the reconstructed end frame — 'Scan' is whole, no descender fragment rides the top edge. Cards land at 0.21-0.61 of the frame; the caption band starts at 0.853 of the canvas, over empty ground.

Portrait: the cards are 0.86 of the plate wide, so the tightest window that still contains them both is 0.90 -> scale 1.549, against the 1.045 the legacy push gives. Modest, but it is the difference between the cards being an element of the page and being the page. The preview reports the window anchored to the bottom canvas edge rather than centred; the picture was checked and the whole title block still fits above the cards.
shots._pointerNote:
The caption is 'Two ways in' and the narration names both of them; 'Scan a room' is the one the film then follows, because the very next scene is that path's onboarding. Clicking the other card and cutting to the AR walkthrough would be a continuity error.

Both coordinates are the centre of the teal card as measured on the committed plate: landscape card x 0.381-0.619 / y 0.518-0.735, portrait card x 0.056-0.916 / y 0.505-0.625. Verified by crosshair crop, not derived.

scenes.caption: One instruction: go slowly.
scenes.narration: It asks you for one thing. Sweep the room slowly, and the map fills in behind you.

shots.alt: Onboarding step two, Sweep the Room Slowly, explaining that moving too fast degrades tracking and that the live point cloud shows what has been covered
shots._focusNote:
The onboarding cards are the only shots in the film where the subject is a small object on a large empty ground. The modal measures w 0.24 x h 0.45 of the plate and sits dead centre; the rest of the 16:9 frame is unlit app shell that carries nothing. Unfocused, the body copy renders at about a 10px x-height on a 1080p frame — technically present, actually unread. The 9:16 cut has no such problem and gets NO focus: the phone frame already crops to the card.

0.64 square at (0.18, 0.18), 2.016x, honoured exactly — deliberately looser than the 0.538 the clamp would allow. At 0.538 (the tightest 16:9 permits) the window anchors and slices the card's icon off the top edge. At 0.60 the whole card fits but 'Skip tutorial' lands on the caption band. 0.64 clears both. Same rect on both cards so they read as one carousel being paged through rather than two unrelated pushes.

Worth stating plainly, because it is the reason these two cards carry the walk beat at all: the onboarding overlay is opaque. Nothing of the xr8 mock's cartoon room is visible behind it — verified against the committed plates, which are flat #0A222E outside the card. These are clean product frames.
shots._pointerNote:
This is the one pointer in the film whose control the caption does not name, and it is here on purpose: the click is not decoration, it is the edit. `what-it-watches` was captured by this shot's own capture config clicking #onboard-next-btn three more times, so the cursor is replaying the interaction that actually produced the next plate. The cut lands on the card the click paged to.

Landscape 0.500/0.590: the pill measures x 0.457-0.543, y 0.578-0.629 on the plate, so this is the upper-middle of the button, deliberately not its centre. At the end of the push the button's lower edge is under the caption band (measured with focus-preview: the band starts at 0.622 of the plate, and the button ends at 0.629); 0.590 keeps the hotspot and its ripple clear of it, and the click fires at 58% of the shot, before the push has finished tightening.

Portrait 0.500/0.615 is the dead centre of the pill (x 0.345-0.655, y 0.585-0.645). There is no portrait focus on this shot, so the phone frame sits at rest and the caption is below it, not over it — no band to clear. Phone frame means a tap ripple rather than a travelling cursor, which the kit chooses off `frame`; nothing is declared here for it.

scenes.caption: Low light, reflections, thin coverage — called out live.
scenes.narration: It watches the light, the reflections and the gaps, and it tells you before you walk out of the room.

shots.alt: Onboarding step four explaining live scan-quality tracking for low light, reflective surfaces and sparse coverage
shots._motionNote: Was `push-in`, which made this shot and `onboard-sweep` the same move over the same rectangle back to back — two pushes at an identical card, which is the 'screenshots being panned' reading this pass exists to remove. `drift-down` opens AT the focus instead of travelling to it, so the cut from `onboard-sweep`'s tight ending is continuous — the carousel pages and the camera stays where it was — and the move then reads down the card, which is what a reader's eye does to a paragraph. There is 0.331 of plate below the focus window, so the drift has room and does not degrade to a push.
shots._focusNote: Same 0.64 rect and the same reasoning as `onboard-sweep` above — see that note. Keeping the two rects identical is what makes the pair read as one carousel.

scenes.caption: One scripted session, two moments. Sparse, then Good.
scenes.narration: Coverage is scored while you walk, off the point count itself. It goes from sparse to good, and the app is the thing that says so.
scenes._editNote:
THE ONLY MOCK FRAME IN THE FILM, AND THE REASON IT IS A `split`.

See the top-level _honestyNote for why the xr8 mock's camera feed cannot be shown as a room. The coverage meter, however, IS the product: #verdict-chip and the COVERAGE bar are computed from pointCloud.count (src/main.ts:726, 751-757), so the difference between these two plates is the app's own accumulation over the same scripted walk — tick 90 against tick 700 — not two staged screenshots.

`split` is the form that makes that honest. Side by side in two browser frames, two identical cartoon rooms read as a controlled comparison rather than as anybody's living room; the eye goes to the thing that CHANGED, which is the meter. Shown one at a time, full-bleed, the same plate reads as 'here is the room I scanned', which is the claim the film must not make. The caption names the session as scripted, on the frame, where the frame is.

`split` is unused fleet-wide; this is the first cut to reach for it. It has no camera and still ignores `motion`. It did also ignore `focus` — silently — and that cost this scene its proof in 16:9: a cell is 42% of the canvas, so the 3840px desktop plate arrives 806px wide and the HUD, a corner overlay covering 17% of the plate, landed about 5px tall on a 1080-tall canvas. The caption says "Sparse, then Good" and nobody could read either word on the frame. The 9:16 cut was fine the whole time, because there the cell holds the 1080px MOBILE plate whose HUD is a full-width banner. video-kit 0.25.0 makes a split cell honour `focus` as a static crop; see the `_focusNote` on the shots.

Both plates keep `mockFreeze` — see capture.config.mjs hazard 1. The freeze is what makes the pair a genuine before-and-after of one session instead of a wall-clock race, and it is also what makes the two plates byte-stable.

shots.alt: The scanning HUD early in a scripted session: a SPARSE badge, 2110 points, a coverage bar reading Low and the app's own recommendation to sweep more slowly
shots._focusNote:
LANDSCAPE ONLY, AND THE SAME RECTANGLE ON BOTH CELLS. A before/after is the comparison; two framings would make it two unrelated pictures.

0.30 square from (0, 0) delivers a window over plate x 0..0.30 by y 0..0.30, which holds the whole HUD (x 0.008..0.185, y 0.012..0.180) with margin down two edges and nothing else. video-kit 0.25.0's floor for a 16:9 split cell is 0.283 of the plate — a cell is 806px of a 3840px capture, so it can crop far tighter than the camera's 0.538 before it starts inventing pixels — and 0.30 sits just above it, honoured exactly rather than capped.

MEASURED, not estimated: crop the committed PNG to 1152x648 at (0,0) and scale it to 806x453, which is exactly what the cell renders, and `SPARSE 2110 pts` / `COVERAGE Low — keep scanning` against `REVIEW 14235 pts` / `COVERAGE Good` come out at about 19px on a 1080-tall canvas. At the uncropped plate they were 5px.

THE CARTOON ROOM LEAVES THE 16:9 FRAME ENTIRELY, and that is a gain rather than a loss. The room is the one thing on this plate that must not read as anybody's living room (see the _honestyNote); the meter is the thing the caption is about. There is no third option — the furniture starts at plate y 0.48, so any window holding both it and the HUD needs y 0.62, which puts the HUD text back under 9px. The room is still in the 9:16 cut, and in the two onboarding scenes before this one.

NO PORTRAIT FOCUS, and this is a measurement rather than an omission. The 9:16 cell loads the MOBILE plate, where the HUD is a full-width banner across the top third; it reads at cell size today. Cropping it would only throw away the walk it is a HUD over.

shots.alt: The same scanning HUD later in the same scripted session, with the point count in the thousands and the coverage bar reading Good
shots._focusNote: The same rectangle as `live-scan-early`, deliberately — see the note there.

scenes.caption: Three rooms, one world — on a machine in your house.
scenes.narration: Every room you scan lands in one world, on a machine in your house. Three rooms here. Sixty-nine thousand points, and fifteen objects that came back named.
scenes._editNote: THIS IS THE SCENE THE FILM'S CENTRAL CLAIM MOVED ONTO. The previous cut made 'Every object named, placed and yours' over the scanner's cartoon feed. Here the same claim is made over a frame that carries its own evidence: the world readout reads 3 scans loaded / 69,046 points / 15 detections, the point clouds are real GLB geometry that went through the real optimize jobs, and plant 89% / sofa 79% / shelf 86% / chair 82% are stored detections with stored confidences. The rooms are generated fixtures rather than a real house — stated in the _honestyNote — but nothing on this frame is drawn by a fixture pretending to be a camera.

shots.alt: The World Editor with three room scans listed in the sidebar, each ready and optimized, the world readout counting 69,046 points and 15 detections, and named objects labelled in the point cloud
shots._motionNote: Was `drift-down`. Every number the caption cites lives in the top-left quadrant — the three scan rows (x 0-0.16, y 0.14-0.37) and the world readout '3 scans loaded / 69,046 points / 15 detections' (x 0.196-0.30, y 0.07-0.145) — so the beat is an arrival on a fact, not a read down a list. It also breaks the drift the previous screen scene ends on.
shots._focusNote:
LANDSCAPE ONLY. The evidence for 'Three rooms. One world. 69,046 points, 15 objects' spans x 0-0.43, y 0.07-0.43 of the plate, which is inside the 0.538 floor, so the floor square is authored directly: scale 2.398, honoured exactly, nothing clamped. The delivered window is x 0-0.538, y 0.049-0.587 — it holds the sidebar's three rows, the world readout, and the left cloud's own labels (plant 89%, sofa 79%, table 95%, shelf 93%, shelf 86%), so the count and the named objects it counts are in one frame.

WHY y IS 0.02 AND NOT 0. See the offset note on `start-screen`: the delivered window sits 0.029 of the plate below the authored y. y 0 would land the window top at 0.029 and slice the Solid / Points / Wire / Semantic mode bar (0.01-0.045) through the middle of its buttons. 0.02 puts the top edge just under it — confirmed on the reconstructed end frame, which opens on 'Companion Scan' and the tab row with the mode bar gone.

THE CAPTION NO LONGER CITES THE READOUT — see this scene's `_captionNote`. The landscape window still holds it, and that is still what this rectangle is for; the change is that the words over the 9:16 cut no longer claim a number that plate does not carry.

NO PORTRAIT FOCUS, and this is a measurement not an omission. The portrait plate drops the world readout entirely and puts a full-width 'Home Office A' detail panel across x 0.47-0.99 at y 0.44-0.585. The tightest portrait window is 0.738, and every 0.738 window that keeps the scan rows readable cuts that panel through its values. A sliced panel reads as a broken render, so the portrait cut keeps its legacy push.

scenes._captionNote:
THE OLD CAPTION READ "Three rooms. One world. 69,046 points, 15 objects." Both numbers are on the LANDSCAPE plate — the world readout at x 0.196..0.30, y 0.07..0.145 — and NEITHER is on the portrait one. viewer.html:952 hides `#hud-info` whenever `#inspector-panel` is visible below 720px, because 171px of readout and a 230px inspector do not both fit across a 360px canvas, and this shot films the inspector open. So in the 9:16 cut the caption cited two figures that appear nowhere on the frame it sits over. One caption is read against both plates; it can only claim what both of them show.

What both plates DO show is the three scan rows — Home Office A, Kitchen A, Living Room A, each "Ready - optimized" — so "three rooms, one world" is carried by the picture in either cut. The second clause is the film's thesis rather than a reading off the screen, which is the same standing the `what-stays-yours` captions have.

THE NARRATION IS UNCHANGED and still says sixty-nine thousand points and fifteen objects. That is a true statement about the product, made over a frame that proves it in 16:9; the bar this edit answers is that a CAPTION must not point at numbers the frame does not carry.

THE BETTER FIX IS A RE-SHOOT, and it is not done here because it is a capture change rather than an edit: closing `#inspector-panel` before the shutter would un-hide `#hud-info` on the mobile plate and put the readout in both cuts. It would also change the LANDSCAPE plate, which currently carries the inspector, so it is a re-capture of this shot in both viewports and a diff to review — not something to smuggle in under a caption fix.

scenes.caption: Not an anonymous cloud of dots.
scenes.narration: The map is not just geometry. Every object keeps the label it was given, and the confidence it was given with.

shots.alt: Semantic view of the same world, colouring the scene by the label attached to each detected object
shots._focusNote:
LANDSCAPE ONLY. The subject is the labels, and nothing else on this plate: the eleven detection chips run x 0.208-0.685, y 0.34-0.632 (plant 89%, sofa 79%, table 95%, shelf 93%, shelf 86%, chair 82%, shelf 72%, chair 78%, plant 77%, lamp 89%, chair 86%). Longest side 0.477, under the 0.538 floor, so the floor square is authored centred on that cluster — window 0.178-0.716 x 0.217-0.755, scale 2.398 exactly. It deliberately starts right of the sidebar (which ends at 0.16): the caption says 'not an anonymous cloud of dots', so the frame should contain the dots and their names and nothing administrative. `drift-down` then travels down through the cluster rather than at it.

NO PORTRAIT FOCUS. Same detail-panel collision as `one-world`: the portrait plate's 'Home Office A' panel sits at x 0.47-0.99 and no 0.738 window keeps both it and the table 95% / shelf 86% labels at x 0.01-0.14 intact.

scenes.caption: Pick a room. The label is yours to correct.
scenes.narration: Pick any room and the camera flies to it. Its name, its confidence and its tags are all yours to change.

shots.alt: The same world after picking the second room from the sidebar: the camera has flown to that scan and the Edit tab has opened on its name, confidence and tags
shots._focusNote:
LANDSCAPE ONLY. The subject is the Edit panel the pick opened — SELECTED OBJECT / Kitchen A at y 0.17, TRANSFORM at 0.285, SEMANTIC TAG and its chip grid from 0.40 down. That column is 0.165 wide, nowhere near the 0.538 floor, so the floor square is authored at x 0, y 0.10. The top edge is picked to include the tab row (SCANS / WORLD / LAYERS / EDIT at y 0.119) so the frame shows WHICH tab the pick landed on, and the bottom at 0.638 keeps the five chip rows above the caption band, which starts at 0.563 of the plate at this framing.

NO PORTRAIT FOCUS AND NO PORTRAIT POINTER. On the portrait plate the panel is full width and the semantic-tag chips are sliced by the viewport at y 0.432 — 'wall floor ceiling window' is rendered as half a row of half chips. There is no honest coordinate for a control that is only half on the plate, so the portrait cut gets neither.
shots._pointerNote:
'The label is yours to correct' — the semantic-tag chips are the control that does the correcting, and the narration names them outright ('its tags are all yours to change'). The cursor lands on `cabinet`, measured at the centre of that chip on the plate and confirmed by crosshair crop; `cabinet` rather than any other because the selected object is Kitchen A, so the tag being reached for should be one a kitchen would take.

At this focus the chip sits at 0.71 of the frame height at the end of the push, with the caption band starting at 0.859 — the ripple (42 canvas px) clears it. The click fires at 58% of the shot, earlier in the push, where the clearance is larger still.

scenes.caption: Preview, Reconstructed, Photoreal — and what the next tier needs.
scenes.narration: Three tiers of map quality, and the app names exactly what the next one would need.

shots.alt: The Layers tab showing the Map Quality stepper — Preview, Reconstructed, Photoreal — with the selected scan's current tier lit and the next step spelled out
shots._motionNote: Was `push-in`, which is what the two preceding world scenes already do. `drift-down` opens on MAP QUALITY at the top of the Layers panel and travels down into what it is made of — Point cloud 49,000 items, Meshes 41 objects, Detections 15 items, Labels 15 items. The tier stepper is the claim; the layer list underneath is the receipt, and the drift is what puts them in one shot in that order.
shots._focusNote:
LANDSCAPE ONLY. MAP QUALITY and its three steps occupy x 0.009-0.152, y 0.19-0.24 — a control about a seventh of the plate wide, so far under the 0.538 floor that the rectangle's shape is irrelevant and the floor square is authored flush left. y 0.02 for the same measured reason as `one-world`: the delivered window sits 0.029 lower than the authored y, and y 0 would slice the mode bar. Delivered window travels 0.049-0.587 to 0.112-0.650 across the drift, which carries the stepper from 0.27-0.36 of the frame up to 0.15-0.24 while the Detections / Labels rows rise out from under the caption band.

NO PORTRAIT FOCUS. The portrait stepper is laid out full width (Preview 0.048-0.34, Reconstructed 0.354-0.646, Photoreal 0.658-0.951) and the caption names all three tiers, so any 0.738 window amputates one of the three words the caption just said. The portrait cut keeps the whole plate — where, in fairness, the stepper is already large.
shots._pointerNote:
The caption's second half is 'and what the next tier needs', so the cursor goes to the NEXT tier — Reconstructed — and not to the lit one. Both coordinates are the centre of that step as measured on their own plate and confirmed by crosshair crop: landscape x 0.059-0.100 / y 0.192-0.240, portrait x 0.354-0.646 / y 0.160-0.219. The two differ because the panel is a narrow rail at 1280px and a full-width row at 360px, which is exactly why `pointer` resolves per format.

Both sit in the upper half of their frame, well clear of the caption band; the landscape drift moves the step further up as the shot runs, not down.

scenes.caption: Nothing to cancel. Nothing to ask for back.
scenes.narration: It runs in the browser on your phone, and it sends the scan to hardware you can point at.
Companion Scan, from Companion Intelligence. UnCloud your life.
